title: Nominal relative clauses and pseudo-clefts
instructions: Choose or type the best answer. Contractions count as two words.
author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)

questions.prompt: ___ the government should do is invest in teacher training.
questions.explanation: *What* = *the thing that*. The clause *What the government should do* is the subject of *is*.

questions.prompt: Everything ___ she told us turned out to be true.
questions.explanation: There is already a noun-like word (*everything*), so you need an ordinary relative (*that*), not *what*.

questions.prompt: ___ wrote this report clearly hadn't looked at the data.
questions.explanation: You need a word meaning *the person who*. Modern English uses *whoever* for this; plain *who* can't start a nominal clause.

questions.prompt: You can sit the exam in May or in June, ___ suits you better.
questions.explanation: There is a fixed set of two choices, so use *whichever* (= the one that).

questions.prompt: ___ hard you try, you won't learn a language in a week.
questions.explanation: *However* + adjective/adverb means *no matter how*. *Whatever* cannot be followed directly by an adjective.
Inside a nominal relative clause, use statement word order (subject + verb), not question word order.

questions.prompt: Complete with TWO words so the meaning stays the same. ‘The thing that worries me is the cost.’ → ‘What ___ is the cost.’
questions.explanation: *What* replaces *the thing that*, so the rest of the clause stays the same: *What worries me is the cost.*

questions.prompt: What I need ___ more time to prepare.
questions.explanation: The *what*-clause is already the subject. Don't add *it*.

questions.prompt: ___ happened was that the deadline was moved forward without warning.
questions.explanation: *What happened was (that)…* is a pseudo-cleft used to introduce an event and focus on it.
